Alpha Blockers Pharmacology: Phenoxybenzamine and Phentolamine Explained

Definition

  • Drugs that competitively or irreversibly blocks the alpha receptors
  • Alpha receptors activation lead to smooth muscle contraction
  • Norepinephrine has higher affinity to alpha receptors compared to epinephrine
  • Alpha 1 receptors are Gq protein coupled located on the vessels walls, iris dilator muscle, prostate, urethral sphincter, pylorus, and anal sphincter and their activation lead to contraction of these smooth muscles
  • Alpha 2 receptors are Gi protein coupled and they located on the sympathetic post ganglionic pre synaptic nerve terminals and when activated they inhibit the release of norepinephrine to the presynaptic

Mechanism of action

  • Blocks alpha adrenoceptors causes decrease in the sympathetic tone of the blood vessels
  • Decreased peripheral vascular resistance and decrease in blood pressure
  • Reflex tachycardia

Phenoxybenzamine

  • Non selective inhibitor
  • Irreversible non competitive inhibition
  • Its effect last until the body synthesize new adrenoceptors which is about 24 hours
  • Therapeutic uses
  • Pheochromocytoma
  • Raynaud disease and frostbite
  • Adverse effects
  • Postural hypotension
  • Cardiac stimulation (more cardiac output and reflex tachycardia)
  • Nasal stuffiness
  • May inhibit ejaculation

Phentolamine

  • Non selective
  • Competitive
  • Last for four hours after single injection
  • Uses
  • Pheochromocytoma
  • Treatment of hypertensive crisis due to abrupt withdrawal of clonidine, clonidine is alpha 2 agonist
  • To reverse local anesthesia in soft tissue sites; local anesthetics are often given with vasoconstrictors that slow their removal. Local phentolamine permits reversal at the end of the procedure
  • Adverse effects
  • Cardiac stimulation (more cardiac output and reflex tachycardia)
  • arrhythmias and anginal pain
